expected_output.reasoning:
The expected root cause is "indeterminate" - the investigation should not confirm an AWS-side impairment, should not recommend simply adding more IOPS/provisioning, should note the clean diagnostic signals (status checks, VolumeStalledIOCheck, AWS Health, FIS), and should point toward escalation to AWS Support if the issue persists.

The investigation summary matches this closely:
- It explicitly states the volume and instance are below their limits ("Instance EBS bandwidth/IOPS limit reached" hypothesis notes "Observed demand is far lower" than the 12,000 IOPS/750 MB/s limit, and the "Volume hitting provisioned IOPS/throughput limit" hypothesis notes the volume ran at ~900/6,000 IOPS, well below provisioned limits).
- It explicitly lists the clean diagnostic signals (status checks, VolumeStalledIOCheck, AWS Health, FIS) and says these "neither confirm nor rule out" an AWS-side issue - i.e., it does not claim certainty of AWS-side impairment.
- It explicitly states: "If the symptom persists with everything below its limits, this is the AWS Support escalation case" - matching the expected guidance to escalate to AWS Support.
- It does not recommend adding more IOPS/provisioning as a fix; instead it frames the saturation hypothesis as inconsistent with the observed pattern (falling IOPS/throughput with rising latency doesn't match a simple cap-hit scenario) and leaves the root cause open among multiple hypotheses (micro-bursting, lazy loading, burst credit exhaustion, AWS-side slowdown), consistent with "the cause stays open."
- It implicitly references the volume status checks and VolumeStalledIOCheck as the direct signals, and references AWS Health as checked (clean).

Overall the investigation correctly lands on "indeterminate," correctly avoids declaring AWS-side impairment or recommending more IOPS, and correctly ties persistence of the issue to AWS Support escalation - matching the expected root cause well.
